879.t: Dancing to rock and roll here and elsewhere
879.s: The Toppers read music; audiences dance everywhere to rock and roll much the same.
879.q: Well, I'd say it's about the same. About the same for that type of music. Yeah, for that type of music, it's about the same.

945.t: How widely jazz was accepted in New Orleans, and by whom
945.s: He thinks most New Orleanians accepted jazz, especially dancers and party-goers, and that devotees were truly enthused. He cannot say what others thought thirty years ago.

154.s: Dancers at the Concerto to End All Concertos and Kenton's advance man and radio promotion.
154.q: We used to play the “Concerto to End All Concertos” and that was like all different tempos. And I swear I’d see people dancing. I don’t know what they were doing but they were dancing. You know you’d have the crowd in the front they were all standing there, and then in the back would be people…

939.t: Saturday night audiences and artists on the same plane as fans
939.s: Interviewer and Brown agree the music let hard-working audiences unwind, with food brought to the dance and artists close to the fans.
939.q: You better believe it. Consequently Louis Jordan came up with tune called “Saturday Night Fish Fry” which was in reality what happened on Saturday night. And when they came out to the dances, as I said, it was something that they prepared for a long time before that. And what they did, not only did…

946.t: Audience of the jazz parties and Dick Gibson
946.s: Rowe and Domber discuss the informed audiences, who grew up with swing, and Condon's publicity.
946.q: Well don’t forget, don’t forget, we were dealing with the jazz parties with a generation that grew up with the music. I mean these were people, for example, who used to see Ralph Sutton at Sunnie’s Rendezvous in Aspen and who used to see these musicians play in the clubs in New York at the time,…

459.t: A concert band booked as a dance band; confusion with Ralph Flanagan
459.s: Wrong agent, puzzled dance audiences, college dates, and RCA confusing Finegan with Flanagan.
459.q: Yeah. They had the wrong booking agent, Willard Alexander, who was used to booking dance bands, and we were not a dance band, we were a concert band for listening. You could dance to us, because Eddie and Bill wrote arrangements which were conducive to dancing, but it was very puzzling to the…

368.t: The disastrous first one-nighter and a riverboat success
368.s: The first New Jersey date flopped because the music was undanceable, but a riverboat date for black audiences went over well.
368.q: Well, we had, I had a whole. We rehearsed and had all this, a library and all this music to play and we’re all of us all good players and ready to take the world on with the band. And we had, I forget the name of the place in New Jersey we were going to play. And on the way there Lenny was next to…

328.t: Playing bebop at dances; Dizzy's band at Sunset Terrace
328.s: Hampton and his brother played bebop at dances to hostile crowds; Dizzy's band later got people dancing at Sunset Terrace.
328.ch: Carnegie Hall, bebop and the big bands
328.q: When you had a dance, you could choose anything you wanted to play at the dance. Most people were probably trying to choose some music that people could dance to and feel comfortable with, more of a swing style. But when my brother and I played, we played bebop at the dances. The people didn’t like…

90.t: How devoted audiences were to the bands
90.s: People saved for weeks to dress for a dance, and many stood listening because radio and records were all there was; he compares Europe.
90.ch: Touring shows and the bands he heard
90.q: Well, I heard all these people, you know. I used to listen to them on the records, you know. It was a really, really nice time, because people were really into the music. Like, people would save up money for weeks to get ready for the dance. They'd be saving for weeks when the bands would come down…

387.s: Dancers came, and Wild Wings in Iowa bewildered them.
387.q: Well, I think you have to realize that there were no groups around touring like that. The people who did come were mostly expecting to dance. It was sold as a dance band, which was unfortunate. We spent most of our time trying to satisfy them but never really doing it.

389.t: Audiences: college crowds versus ballroom dancers
389.s: College students listened closely while ballroom dancers just danced fox trots.
389.ch: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
389.q: that was something else again. The bands never enjoyed that in those days, seldom, unless you played colleges. Those college kids, they'd be get right up front and listening and listen to the band and talking to the musicians. You'd they'd get a big kick out of that.
